characters: Esenam: an attentive eight-year-old Ghanaian girl with braided puff buns, wearing a coral T-shirt under a patterned kitchen apron.
Karim: her nine-year-old Ghanaian cousin with short curly hair, wearing a green collared polo shirt and denim shorts.
Esenam’s mother: a warm Ghanaian woman in an indigo-and-amber African-print dress.
Their teacher: a kind Ghanaian woman wearing a teal blouse and patterned skirt.

narrationPlan.voice: A bright girl’s voice for Esenam; a calm boy’s voice for Karim; a clear teacher voice
narrationPlan.pace: Practical and clear, with a firm safety ending (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A calm tune with a sieve-shaking rhythm (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Sorting stones from rice and sieving are everyday kitchen tasks in many Ghanaian homes. The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on mixtures and their separation (B2.1.2.3, B3.1.2.2) and on water as a natural resource (B2.2.1.4, B3.2.1.4).
The story is clear that cloth filtering does not make water safe to drink. Only an adult boils or treats water for drinking.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check that the safety ending is clear: filtering through cloth does not make unsafe water safe.
Check the separation methods (picking, sieving, settling, filtering) against the NaCCA standards.

teacherGuide.overview: Two kitchen examples show how to separate mixtures, first solids from solids, then a solid from a liquid. It ends with a safety lesson on drinking water. Based on NaCCA Science standards on mixtures and on water as a resource.
learningGoals: Name four ways to separate mixtures.
Say why clear water may not be safe.
beforeReading: Ask: what is mixed together in your home or school?
whileReading: Pause on page 5 and ask: why is the clear water still not safe?
afterReading: Make a mixture of sand and rice and separate it with a sieve.
Settle and filter muddy water, then label it “not safe to drink”.
discussion: Which method would you use for sand and water?
How do we make water safe to drink?
reflection: Where does your drinking water come from?

support: Use pictures of each step and put them in order.
stretch: Compare filtering through a cloth, paper and a sieve.

culturalNotes: Sorting stones from rice and sieving are everyday kitchen tasks in many Ghanaian homes. The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on mixtures and their separation (B2.1.2.3, B3.1.2.2) and on water as a natural resource (B2.2.1.4, B3.2.1.4).
The story is clear that cloth filtering does not make water safe to drink. Only an adult boils or treats water for drinking.
localiseThis: Use the rice, beans, gari or other foods that children know.
Remind children never to drink water that has not been made safe by an adult.
